prompt: You compare two implementations with a steady-state benchmark. Which practices make the result more trustworthy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run each version many times and compare the distributions (or the minimum, for a micro-benchmark)
options.explanation: Correct. Repeated measurements expose variation and make a comparison more credible; they do not automatically remove bias or all noise.

options.text: Use input sizes similar to production
options.explanation: Correct. Complexity differences only show at scale; an O(n²) algorithm can look fine on 100 items.

options.text: Include a warm-up phase before measuring
options.explanation: Correct. Cold caches, lazy imports, connection setup and JIT compilation distort the first iterations.

options.text: Run the old version on your laptop and the new one on a CI server
options.explanation: Different hardware and load confound the effect of the code change. Use comparable environments or a carefully designed normalisation instead of attributing the difference to the implementation alone.

options.text: Run the benchmark once and report the number to three decimal places
options.explanation: Extra decimal places do not establish accuracy. A single measurement gives no useful estimate of variability.

workedExample:
A fair benchmark changes only one thing: the code under test.

- Same machine, same data, same conditions (rules out D).
- Realistic data sizes (B).
- Warm-up, then many repetitions (A, C).
- Report a range or a robust statistic, not one number (rules out E).

The `timeit` docs suggest using the minimum of repeated runs for snippets, since slower runs are usually caused by interference rather than the code itself.

prompt: Your load test reports a p99 latency of 40 ms. Production users report frequent multi-second waits under the same request rate. The load generator uses 10 threads, each sending a request and waiting for the response before sending the next. Which statements are true? Select all that apply. Assume production arrivals continue independently while earlier requests wait.

options.text: When the server stalls, the generator stops sending requests, so the slow period contributes few samples and the percentiles look better than reality
options.explanation: Correct. This is coordinated omission: the tool unintentionally coordinates with the system under test and omits the requests that would have queued up.

options.text: A constant-rate load generator that records latency from each request's intended send time gives a more honest p99
options.explanation: Correct. Tools like wrk2 schedule requests at a fixed rate, so a stall shows up as many slow requests, as it would for real users.

options.text: The mean latency would have been a better metric than p99
options.explanation: The mean hides tail latency even more. The problem is how samples were collected, not which statistic was used.

options.text: The difference must be caused by the production network, since load tests are always accurate
options.explanation: Closed-loop load generators systematically under-report tail latency during stalls; the test itself is a likely cause of the discrepancy.

workedExample:
1. Under the specified production model, requests arrive independently: if the server stalls for 2 s, requests keep arriving and all wait.
2. A closed-loop generator with 10 threads sends at most 10 requests during that stall. Hundreds of 'would-have-been' slow requests are never sent.
3. Result: the stall contributes maybe 10 slow samples out of 100,000, so p99 looks fine.
4. Fix: use an open-loop load generator at a constant rate and measure latency from the scheduled send time.
